grammar.title: 1. Động từ be: am, is, are
grammar.explain: Động từ be (là, thì, ở) thay đổi theo chủ ngữ. I đi với am. He, She, It đi với is. You, We, They đi với are. Câu phủ định thêm not sau be: I am not a teacher. She is not from Hanoi.
examples: I am a student. — Tôi là học sinh.
She is Vietnamese. — Cô ấy là người Việt Nam.
They are my friends. — Họ là bạn của tôi.
We are not teachers. — Chúng tôi không phải là giáo viên.
grammar.lesson: Chào hỏi và giới thiệu bản thân

grammar.title: 2. Hỏi tên và giới thiệu bản thân
grammar.explain: Hỏi tên: What is your name? (Tên bạn là gì?). Trả lời: My name is + tên. Hỏi quê quán: Where are you from? (Bạn đến từ đâu?). Trả lời: I am from + nơi chốn. Chú ý: What is viết tắt là What's, I am viết tắt là I'm.
examples: What is your name? — My name is Minh. (Tên bạn là gì? — Tên tôi là Minh.)
Where are you from? — I am from Hanoi. (Bạn đến từ đâu? — Tôi đến từ Hà Nội.)
Nice to meet you! — Nice to meet you too! (Rất vui được gặp bạn! — Tôi cũng vậy!)
grammar.lesson: Chào hỏi và giới thiệu bản thân

grammar.title: 1. Sở hữu cách: 's
grammar.explain: Để nói một người hay một vật thuộc về ai, thêm 's vào tên người đó: Lan's mother = mẹ của Lan; Nam's father = bố của Nam. Với tên kết thúc bằng s, chỉ thêm dấu phẩy trên: James' book = sách của James.
examples: Lan's mother is a teacher. — Mẹ của Lan là giáo viên.
This is Nam's sister. — Đây là em gái của Nam.
My father's name is Hung. — Tên bố tôi là Hùng.
grammar.lesson: Gia đình của tôi — My Family

grammar.title: 2. Tính từ sở hữu: my, your, his, her, our, their
grammar.explain: Tính từ sở hữu đứng TRƯỚC danh từ và không bao giờ thêm s: my mother (mẹ của tôi), his father (bố của anh ấy), her brother (anh trai của cô ấy), our family (gia đình của chúng tôi), their house (nhà của họ). Không nói 'the my mother' — chỉ dùng một từ sở hữu.
examples: This is my family. — Đây là gia đình của tôi.
Her brother is a student. — Anh trai của cô ấy là học sinh.
Our parents are teachers. — Bố mẹ của chúng tôi là giáo viên.
grammar.lesson: Gia đình của tôi — My Family

grammar.title: 1. some và any
grammar.explain: some dùng trong câu khẳng định và lời mời: I have some bread. Would you like some tea? any dùng trong câu phủ định và câu hỏi: I don't have any milk. Do you have any eggs? Với danh từ đếm được số ít, dùng a/an: an egg, a cup of tea.
examples: I have some rice. — Tôi có một ít cơm.
I don't have any coffee. — Tôi không có cà phê.
Would you like some juice? — Bạn có muốn uống chút nước ép không?
Do you have any bread? — Bạn có bánh mì không?
grammar.lesson: Món ăn và đồ uống — Food and Drink

grammar.title: 2. I like / I don't like
grammar.explain: Nói sở thích: I like + danh từ hoặc động từ thêm ing: I like tea. I like eating noodles. Phủ định: I don't like + danh từ/ing: I don't like fish. Câu hỏi: Do you like coffee? — Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
examples: I like chicken. — Tôi thích thịt gà.
I don't like fish. — Tôi không thích cá.
Do you like tea? — Yes, I do. — Bạn có thích trà không? — Có.
She likes fruit, but she doesn't like meat. — Cô ấy thích trái cây, nhưng không thích thịt.
grammar.lesson: Món ăn và đồ uống — Food and Drink

grammar.title: 1. There is / There are
grammar.explain: There is + danh từ số ít: There is a table in the kitchen. There are + danh từ số nhiều: There are two chairs in the room. Câu hỏi: Is there a garden? — Yes, there is. Are there any windows? — Yes, there are.
examples: There is a sofa in the living room. — Có một ghế sofa trong phòng khách.
There are two bedrooms in my house. — Có hai phòng ngủ trong nhà tôi.
Is there a garden? — Yes, there is. — Có vườn không? — Có.
There isn't a TV in my bedroom. — Không có ti-vi trong phòng ngủ của tôi.
grammar.lesson: Nhà của tôi — My Home

grammar.title: 2. Giới từ chỉ vị trí: in, on, under, next to, between
grammar.explain: in = trong, on = trên mặt, under = dưới, next to = bên cạnh, between = ở giữa hai vật: The book is on the table. The cat is under the chair. The lamp is next to the bed. The table is between the sofa and the window.
examples: The book is on the table. — Quyển sách ở trên bàn.
The cat is under the chair. — Con mèo ở dưới cái ghế.
The kitchen is next to the living room. — Nhà bếp ở bên cạnh phòng khách.
The lamp is between the bed and the window. — Cái đèn ở giữa giường và cửa sổ.
grammar.lesson: Nhà của tôi — My Home

grammar.title: 1. Hỏi và nói giờ
grammar.explain: Hỏi giờ: What time is it? (Mấy giờ rồi?). Trả lời bắt đầu bằng It is... Giờ chẵn: o'clock (3 o'clock = 3 giờ). 30 phút: half past (half past five = 5 giờ 30). 15 phút: quarter past (quarter past nine = 9 giờ 15); 45 phút: quarter to (quarter to eight = 8 giờ kém 15, tức 7 giờ 45).
examples: It is three o'clock. — Bây giờ là 3 giờ.
It is half past five. — Bây giờ là 5 giờ rưỡi.
It is quarter past nine. — Bây giờ là 9 giờ 15 phút.
It is quarter to eight. — Bây giờ là 7 giờ 45 phút (8 giờ kém 15).
grammar.lesson: Số đếm, ngày và giờ

grammar.title: 2. Các thứ trong tuần và giới từ on
grammar.explain: Hỏi thứ: What day is it today? Trả lời: It is + thứ trong tuần. Khi nói làm việc gì vào thứ nào, dùng giới từ on trước thứ: on Monday, on Friday. Các thứ trong tuần luôn viết hoa chữ cái đầu: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
examples: What day is it today? — It is Monday. (Hôm nay là thứ mấy? — Hôm nay là thứ Hai.)
I go to school on Monday. (Tôi đi học vào thứ Hai.)
We have English on Tuesday and Friday. (Chúng tôi học tiếng Anh vào thứ Ba và thứ Sáu.)
grammar.lesson: Số đếm, ngày và giờ

grammar.title: 1. be going to: kế hoạch tương lai
grammar.explain: be going to + động từ nguyên thể nói về kế hoạch đã quyết định: I am going to travel to Da Nang. She is going to stay at a hotel. Câu hỏi: Are you going to visit Hue? — Yes, I am.
examples: I am going to travel to Da Nang next month. — Tôi sẽ đi du lịch Đà Nẵng vào tháng tới.
She is going to stay at a hotel. — Cô ấy sẽ ở khách sạn.
Are you going to visit Hue? — Yes, I am. — Bạn có định thăm Huế không? — Có.
grammar.lesson: Du lịch và kỳ nghỉ — Travel and Holidays

grammar.title: 2. Thì quá khứ đơn: kể chuyến đi đã qua
grammar.explain: Quá khứ đơn kể chuyện đã xảy ra: We visited Ha Long Bay last year. Động từ có quy tắc thêm ed (visit thành visited, stay thành stayed); động từ bất quy tắc đổi dạng (go thành went, buy thành bought, take thành took). Câu hỏi: Did you have a good trip? — Yes, I did.
examples: We visited Ha Long Bay last year. — Năm ngoái chúng tôi đã thăm vịnh Hạ Long.
She bought two tickets yesterday. — Hôm qua cô ấy đã mua hai vé.
Did you have a good trip? — Yes, I did. — Bạn đã có chuyến đi vui vẻ chứ? — Có.
grammar.lesson: Du lịch và kỳ nghỉ — Travel and Holidays

grammar.title: 1. Thì hiện tại đơn nói về thói quen
grammar.explain: Thì hiện tại đơn (Present Simple) dùng để nói về thói quen hằng ngày và sự thật hiển nhiên. Với chủ ngữ I, You, We, They: động từ giữ nguyên. Với chủ ngữ He, She, It: động từ thêm s hoặc es (get thành gets, watch thành watches, study thành studies). Câu hỏi: Do you get up early? — Yes, I do. / Does she get up early? — Yes, she does.
examples: I get up at six o'clock. — Tôi thức dậy lúc 6 giờ.
She gets up at six o'clock. — Cô ấy thức dậy lúc 6 giờ.
He watches TV in the evening. — Anh ấy xem ti-vi vào buổi tối.
They go to work at eight. — Họ đi làm lúc 8 giờ.
grammar.lesson: Everyday English — Tiếng Anh hằng ngày

grammar.title: 2. Trạng từ tần suất: always, usually, often, sometimes, never
grammar.explain: Trạng từ tần suất nói bạn làm việc gì thường xuyên đến mức nào: always (luôn luôn, 100%), usually (thường thường, 80%), often (thường, 60%), sometimes (thỉnh thoảng, 40%), never (không bao giờ, 0%). Vị trí: đứng TRƯỚC động từ thường (I usually get up) nhưng đứng SAU động từ be (He is always late).
examples: I always get up at six. — Tôi luôn thức dậy lúc 6 giờ.
She usually has breakfast at home. — Cô ấy thường ăn sáng ở nhà.
He is always late. — Anh ấy luôn đi muộn.
We never watch TV in the morning. — Chúng tôi không bao giờ xem ti-vi vào buổi sáng.
grammar.lesson: Everyday English — Tiếng Anh hằng ngày

grammar.title: 1. Hỏi giá: How much is it?
grammar.explain: Hỏi giá: How much is + danh từ số ít? (How much is this shirt?). Hỏi giá số nhiều: How much are + danh từ số nhiều? (How much are these shoes?). Trả lời: It is + giá (số ít) hoặc They are + giá (số nhiều). Chú ý: hỏi giá tiền luôn dùng How much, không dùng How many (How many chỉ dùng để hỏi số lượng đếm được: How many books? = Có bao nhiêu quyển sách?).
examples: How much is this shirt? — It is 150,000 dong. (Cái áo này giá bao nhiêu? — 150.000 đồng.)
How much are these shoes? — They are 300,000 dong. (Đôi giày này giá bao nhiêu? — 300.000 đồng.)
How much is that book? — It is 50,000 dong. (Quyển sách kia giá bao nhiêu? — 50.000 đồng.)
grammar.lesson: Đi mua sắm và hỏi giá

grammar.title: 2. this/that/these/those
grammar.explain: this (cái này) và these (những cái này) chỉ thứ ở GẦN người nói. that (cái kia) và those (những cái kia) chỉ thứ ở XA người nói. Số ít dùng this/that + is; số nhiều dùng these/those + are. Ví dụ: This is my bag. (Đây là túi của tôi.) That is your book. (Kia là sách của bạn.)
examples: This shirt is cheap. — Cái áo này rẻ.
That shirt is expensive. — Cái áo kia đắt.
These shoes are beautiful. — Những đôi giày này đẹp.
Those pens are blue. — Những cây bút kia màu xanh.
grammar.lesson: Đi mua sắm và hỏi giá

grammar.title: 1. should / shouldn't: lời khuyên
grammar.explain: should + động từ nguyên thể đưa ra lời khuyên: You should drink more water. shouldn't = should not: You shouldn't smoke. Câu hỏi: Should I stay at home? — Yes, you should.
examples: You should drink more water. — Bạn nên uống nhiều nước hơn.
You shouldn't smoke. — Bạn không nên hút thuốc.
Should I take this medicine? — Yes, you should. — Tôi có nên uống thuốc này không? — Có.
grammar.lesson: Sức khỏe và cơ thể — Health and Body

grammar.title: 2. have a + tên bệnh
grammar.explain: Nói mình bị bệnh: have a + headache (đau đầu), cold (cảm lạnh), cough (ho), fever (sốt), stomachache (đau bụng), toothache (đau răng). Chú ý: a headache, a cold, a fever — luôn có a. Hỏi thăm: What's the matter? — I have a headache.
examples: I have a headache. — Tôi bị đau đầu.
She has a cold. — Cô ấy bị cảm lạnh.
What's the matter? — I have a fever. — Có chuyện gì vậy? — Tôi bị sốt.
grammar.lesson: Sức khỏe và cơ thể — Health and Body

grammar.title: 1. What is the weather like?
grammar.explain: Hỏi thời tiết: What is the weather like today? Trả lời ngắn: It is sunny. / It is rainy. / It is cold. / It is windy. Cũng có thể nói: The weather is nice today. (Thời tiết hôm nay đẹp.)
examples: What is the weather like today? — Hôm nay thời tiết thế nào?
It is sunny and warm. — Trời nắng và ấm.
It is cold in winter. — Mùa đông trời lạnh.
grammar.lesson: Thời tiết và các mùa — Weather and Seasons

grammar.title: 2. Thì hiện tại tiếp diễn nói thời tiết
grammar.explain: It is raining (trời đang mưa), It is snowing (trời đang có tuyết). Cấu trúc: It + is + V-ing. So sánh: It rains a lot in autumn (thói quen, hiện tại đơn) và It is raining now (đang diễn ra, hiện tại tiếp diễn).
examples: It is raining now. — Trời đang mưa.
It rains a lot in autumn. — Mùa thu trời mưa nhiều.
Look! The sun is shining. — Nhìn kìa! Mặt trời đang chiếu sáng.
grammar.lesson: Thời tiết và các mùa — Weather and Seasons

grammar.title: 3. Các mùa dùng với in
grammar.explain: Tên mùa đi với giới từ in: in spring, in summer, in autumn, in winter. Tên mùa không dùng mạo từ the khi nói chung: I like autumn. (Không nói I like the autumn.)
examples: In summer, we go swimming. — Mùa hè chúng tôi đi bơi.
In winter, it is cold. — Mùa đông trời lạnh.
I like spring best. — Tôi thích mùa xuân nhất.
grammar.lesson: Thời tiết và các mùa — Weather and Seasons

grammar.title: Present perfect: since/for, already/yet; present perfect vs past simple
grammar.explain:
Structure: have/has + past participle — I have read; she has studied; they have lived. The present perfect connects the past to NOW. Use it for a past action with a result that matters today, or for an experience in your life up to now.

Rule 1: since + a point in time; for + a length of time I have believed in Jesus since 2018 (a point: 2018). — We have studied the Sermon on the Mount for three weeks (a length: three weeks). Other points: since Monday, since I was a child, since last year. Other lengths: for five years, for a long time, for two days.

Rule 2: already (affirmative) and yet (negative and question) I have already read the Beatitudes twice this week. — She has already memorized Matthew 5:3. I have not memorized them yet. — Have you read the Sermon on the Mount yet? Already goes before the main verb; yet goes at the end.

Rule 3: Present perfect vs past simple — finished time or not? Use the past simple when the time is FINISHED: Jesus taught the Sermon on the Mount about two thousand years ago. — They visited the church last Sunday. Use the present perfect when NO finished time is given and the result matters now: I have read the Beatitudes twice this week. — Have you ever been to a Bible study on a mountain? Signal words for the past simple: yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago. Signal words for the present perfect: ever, never, already, yet, since, for, this week (the week is not finished).
grammar.lesson: Bài 1: Bài Giảng Trên Núi

grammar.title: Past perfect (had + past participle); past perfect vs past simple in narrative
grammar.explain:
Form: had + past participle — had chosen, had waited, had already looked, had given. The past perfect describes the earlier of two past actions. Think of a timeline: the past perfect is the action that happened first, further back in the past; the past simple is the action that happened second, closer to now.

Structure 1: “By the time + past simple, … had + past participle” “By the time Samuel arrived, Jesse had already presented seven sons.” — Samuel’s arrival is the later past moment; Jesse’s presenting happened before it. “By the time Goliath fell, David had thrown only one stone.” Use already before the participle to stress that the earlier action was complete: had already chosen, had already promised.

Structure 2: “After / Before” with two past actions “David repented after Nathan had told him the truth.” (Nathan’s telling came first.) “Samuel anointed David after God had rejected Saul.” With after, the past perfect follows it; with before, the past perfect comes first: “Before David became king, he had looked after his father’s sheep for many years.”

Structure 3: Past perfect vs. past simple — don’t mix them up Past simple = a finished action in the past: “David killed Goliath.” Past perfect = an action finished before another past action: “David had killed a lion and a bear before he fought Goliath.” In a story, use the past simple for the main events and the past perfect only to “step back” and explain what had happened earlier. If you use the past perfect for everything, your story sounds wrong — use it like a flashback, not like the main plot. Common mistakes: (1) Forgetting had: “God chosen David” — wrong; say “God had chosen David.” (2) Past perfect for a single past event: “David had killed Goliath yesterday” — wrong; say “David killed Goliath.” (3) Base verb after had: “had choose” — wrong; say “had chosen.”
grammar.lesson: Bài 2: Cuộc Đời Đa-vít

grammar.title: Passive voice (present/past simple passive; passive with by)
grammar.explain:
Form: be + past participle. Present simple: am / is / are + past participle — "Forgiveness is given freely." Past simple: was / were + past participle — "He was wounded for our transgressions." The by-phrase names the agent: "He was despised by men." — "Our iniquity was laid on Him by the Lord." Active to passive: move the object to the front, and the subject goes to the end with by (or disappears). Active: "Men despised Him." Passive: "He was despised by men." Active: "God invites the thirsty." Passive: "The thirsty are invited by God."

When to use the passive — three reasons: 1. The receiver matters more than the doer: "He was wounded for us" — the focus is on the Servant, not on who wounded Him. Bible English loves the passive for this reason. 2. The doer is unknown or unimportant: "The invitation was written in Isaiah 55" — who wrote it does not matter here. 3. The doer is God, and the focus is on grace: "We are saved by grace" — the gift matters, not our part in it.

Watch out: do not use the passive when the doer is the point: "Isaiah wrote these words" is better than "These words were written by Isaiah." And never forget the be verb: say "He was wounded", not "He wounded".
grammar.lesson: Bài 3: Các Tiên Tri: Ê-sai

grammar.title: Relative clauses: who / which / that; defining vs non-defining
grammar.explain:
A relative clause is a small sentence inside a sentence. It begins with a relative pronoun — who, which, or that — and it describes a noun: "The friend who gave me wise counsel is a true friend." "The lamp which guides my feet is God's word." "The path that leads to life is narrow." Which pronoun? Use who for people: "the man who meditates on God's law". Use which for things: "the law which makes wise the simple". Use that for people or things: "the counsel that you gave me" / "the tree that stands by the water". Defining clauses (no commas) tell us which one — the information is essential. "The friend who tells the truth is a treasure." (Which friend? The one who tells the truth.) Without the clause, we do not know which friend is meant. Non-defining clauses (with commas) add extra information about someone we already know. "Solomon, who was the son of David, asked God for wisdom." (We already know who Solomon is; the clause is a bonus. You can remove it and the sentence still works.) Note: that is never used in a non-defining clause — say "Solomon, who was the son of David", never "Solomon, that was...".

Watch out: never use which for a person ("the man which meditates" is wrong — use who), and never drop the pronoun when it is the subject of the clause: "The man who meditates on God's law is blessed" — not "The man meditates on God's law is blessed".
grammar.lesson: Bài 4: Sự Khôn Ngoan: Châm Ngôn & Thi Thiên

grammar.title: Second conditional (If + past simple, would + base verb); wishes and hypotheticals
grammar.explain:
Form: If + past simple, would + base verb. "If we were justified by works, grace would not be grace." — "If Abraham had been justified by works, he would have something to boast about." Use were (not was) after if for all persons in formal English: "If I were still under the law…" ("If I was…" is common in speech, but were is correct in writing.)

Meaning: the second conditional talks about unreal or imaginary situations — things that are not true now, or that we are only imagining. Paul uses it to show why salvation cannot be by works: "If we were justified by works" — but we are not! We are justified by faith.

Compare the first conditional (real future): "If you believe, you will have peace" — with the second (imaginary): "If you believed, you would have peace."

Wishes — the same past-simple form after wish: I wish + past simple — a wish about the present that is not true: "I wish I had peace with God." (I do not have it yet.) — "I wish I trusted Christ more." — "I wish I were sure of my salvation."

Note: wish takes were too: "I wish I were free from fear."

Would in the result clause: the main clause always uses would (not will): "If we trusted in our works, we would never know if we had done enough."

Short forms in speech: "If I trusted Him, I'd have peace."

Watch out: never use would in the If-clause: say "If we were justified by works…", not "If we would be justified…". And never use will in the result: say "…grace would not be grace", not "…grace will not be grace".
grammar.lesson: Bài 5: Rô-ma: Được Xưng Công Chính Bởi Đức Tin

grammar.title: Reported speech: statements (say/tell + that-clause, tense backshift), questions (ask + if/whether/wh-word), commands (tell/ask + to-infinitive)
grammar.explain:
When we tell someone what another person said, we usually shift the tense back one step — because the words were spoken in the past. This is called reported speech (or indirect speech).

Structure 1: Reported Statements — say / tell + that Direct: Jesus said, “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed.” Reported: Jesus said that the kingdom of heaven was like a mustard seed. (In Bible retelling, the present tense is often kept when the truth is still true: “Jesus said that the kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed” is also correct.) Use say with no person, and tell with a person: “He said that he would return.” — “He told his servants that he would return.” Never say “He said me that…” Backshift table — direct speech to reported speech: Present simple to past simple: “The seed is the word of God.” to “The teacher said that the seed was the word of God.”

Present continuous to past continuous: “The thorns are growing.” to “He said that the thorns were growing.” Will to would: “I will return.” to “The master said that he would return.” Can to could: “I can explain it.” to “Hoa said that she could explain it.” Present perfect to past perfect: “I have found the treasure.” to “He said that he had found the treasure.”

Structure 2: Reported Questions — ask + if / whether / Wh-word Yes/No questions use if or whether, and the word order becomes statement order (no do / does / did, no question mark): Direct: “Is the kingdom like a pearl?” Reported: “Lan asked if the kingdom was like a pearl.” Wh-questions keep the question word: Direct: “What does the parable mean?” Reported: “The disciple asked what the parable meant.”

Structure 3: Reported Commands — tell / ask + person + to + verb Direct: “Watch and be ready.” Reported: “Jesus told the disciples to watch and be ready.” Direct: “Use my money well.” Reported: “The master told his servants to use his money well.” For a negative command, use not to: “Do not be afraid” to “He told them not to be afraid.”

Watch out: do not keep the question word order in reported questions — say “He asked what the parable meant”, not “He asked what did the parable mean”. And remember: say takes no person (“He said that…”), tell always takes a person (“He told me that…”).
grammar.lesson: Bài 6: Các Dụ Ngôn Về Nước Thiên Đàng

grammar.title: Phrasal verbs: come upon, fill with, speak out, stand up, pour out, break out; separable vs inseparable, with the object pronoun rule
grammar.explain:
A phrasal verb is a verb + a small word (a particle, like up, out, upon) that together have a new meaning. Pour means to tip liquid from a container; pour out means to give freely and in full measure — God poured out His Spirit. The six phrasal verbs of this lesson all come from Acts: come upon — to arrive and rest on someone: "The Holy Spirit came upon the believers." fill with — to make full of something: "God filled them with boldness." stand up — to rise to your feet: "Peter stood up and spoke." speak out — to speak boldly and openly: "Do not be afraid to speak out about Jesus." pour out — to give freely and in full measure: "God poured out His Spirit on all people." break out — to start suddenly: "Great joy broke out in the city." Separable phrasal verbs — the object can go in the middle pour out and speak out are separable: the object can go between the verb and the particle, or after the whole verb. Both are correct: "God poured out His Spirit on all people." — "God poured His Spirit out on all people." And: "They spoke out the word boldly." — "They spoke the word out boldly." Inseparable phrasal verbs — nothing goes in the middle come upon, fill with and break out are inseparable: the object must come after the whole verb, never in the middle. Say "The Spirit came upon them", never "came them upon". Say "God filled them with power", never "filled with them power". Say "Joy broke out in the city", never "broke in the city out". stand up usually takes no object at all: "Peter stood up."

The object pronoun rule — the most important rule When the object is a pronoun (it, them, him, her, us), the rule becomes strict. With a separable verb, the pronoun must go between the verb and the particle: "God poured it out on all people." — never "poured out it". "They spoke it out boldly." — never "spoke out it". With an inseparable verb, the pronoun stays after the whole verb: "The Spirit came upon them." — "God filled them with power."

Watch out: Vietnamese has no phrasal verbs, so learners often put the pronoun in the wrong place ("poured out it") or split an inseparable verb ("came them upon"). Ask two questions: (1) Can this verb split at all? (2) Is my object a pronoun? If the verb splits and the object is a pronoun, the pronoun goes in the middle — always.
grammar.lesson: Bài 7: Đức Thánh Linh Trong Sách Công Vụ Các Sứ Đồ

grammar.title: Modals — advice (should / ought to), obligation (must / have to), possibility (might / may / could); prohibition (mustn't) vs no obligation (don't have to)
grammar.explain:
Modal verbs (should, ought to, must, have to, might, may, could) show the speaker's attitude: is this good advice, a duty, or only a possibility? The modal is always followed by the base verb (no -s, no to) — except ought to, which keeps its to. The form never changes for he / she / it: “He should pray”, not “He should prays”.

Structure 1: Advice — should / ought to (something is a good idea) “We should pray every day.” — “We ought to worship God with a sincere heart.” — “You should thank God for His goodness before you ask for more.” Ought to is a little stronger and more formal than should, and it is common in Bible teaching. Note the form: should + base verb but ought to + base verb. Never say “You should to pray” or “We ought worship”.

Structure 2: Obligation — must / have to (something is necessary) “True worshipers must worship the Father in spirit and truth.” (John 4:24) — “Christians have to gather together to worship God.” (Heb 10:25) Must is the speaker's own strong command — Jesus Himself uses it in John 4:24. Have to is an obligation that comes from outside — a rule, a situation, or someone else. In the negative they are very different: mustn't means “do not do it” (“We mustn't worship with a proud heart”), but don't have to means “it is not necessary” (“You don't have to pray for a long time — a short, sincere prayer is precious”).

Structure 3: Possibility & Permission — might / may / could “God might answer our prayer in a way we do not expect.” — “You may come to the prayer meeting tonight if you are free.” — “You could begin with a simple prayer.” Might shows a small possibility (less sure than may); may gives permission; could offers a gentle suggestion or a possibility. All three take the base verb: “God might answer”, not “God might answers”. Modal strength — from weakest to strongest: might / could (maybe) — may (permission / possibility) — should / ought to (good advice) — have to (necessary, from outside) — must (necessary, the speaker's command).

Watch out: never use to after should, must, might, may, could; only ought to and have to keep the to.
grammar.lesson: Bài 8: Cầu Nguyện Và Thờ Phượng

grammar.title: Gerunds and infinitives: verb + -ing (enjoy, love, stop + -ing) vs verb + to-infinitive (want, decide, hope, called us to love); verbs with meaning change: stop, remember
grammar.explain:
A gerund is a verb with -ing used as a noun: “Serving together is a joy.” An infinitive is to + verb: “God called us to love one another.” Some verbs are followed by a gerund, some by an infinitive — and the choice is fixed, so you must learn which verbs take which form.

Structure 1: Verb + Gerund (-ing) Use the gerund after these verbs: enjoy, love, hate, like, finish, practise, stop, start, keep, mind, suggest, avoid. Examples: “We enjoy serving together.” — “She loves encouraging her friends.” — “He stopped worrying about his gift.” After a preposition, always use the gerund: “Thank you for helping me.” — “We grow by serving together.”

Structure 2: Verb + to-Infinitive Use the infinitive after these verbs: want, decide, hope, plan, need, learn, choose, promise, try, remember, forget. Examples: “God called us to love one another.” — “I decided to help with the Sunday school.” — “They hope to grow up into maturity.” — “We want to build up the body of Christ.” The infinitive also shows purpose — why we do something: “Christ gave gifts to equip the saints.” — “We meet to worship God together.”

Structure 3: Verbs That Take Both — With a Change of Meaning Stop: stop + -ing means quit doing it: “I stopped worrying.” (I do not worry any more.) Stop + to + verb means stop in order to do something else: “We stopped to pray.” (We stopped our walk in order to pray.) Remember: remember + -ing means remember a past action: “I remember singing in the choir.” (I sang, and I remember it.) Remember + to + verb means do not forget to do something in the future: “Remember to pray for our pastors.” (Do not forget to pray.)

Watch out: never say “I enjoy to serve” (use serving) and never say “I want serving” (use to serve). A useful trick: learn the verb and its form together — enjoy serving, want to serve — as one pair, not as two separate words.
grammar.lesson: Bài 9: Hội Thánh: Một Thân Thể

grammar.title: Used to / would for past habits (used to + verb for habits and states; would + verb only for repeated actions; did not use to for negatives); future perfect intro (will have + past participle with by + future time)
grammar.explain:
Structure 1: Used to + Verb — Past Habits and Past States We use used to + verb for a habit or a state in the past that is no longer true now: “I used to worry about money all the time.” (I worried then; I do not worry now.) — “We used to be very poor.” (We were poor then; we are not poor now.) The negative is did not use to (note: use, not used): “We did not use to have a car.” The question is Did you use to…?: “Did you use to worry about money?”

Structure 2: Would + Verb — Repeated Past Actions Only We use would + verb for a repeated action in the past: “Every Sunday, my father would count the money for the week.” — “Every month, my grandmother would save a little money.” But would is only for actions, never for states. We cannot say “I would be poor” or “I would worry about money” for a state — for states, use used to: “I used to be poor.” — “I used to worry about money.” Test: if you can add “every Sunday” to the action, would is possible; for a feeling or a state, only used to works.

Structure 3: Future Perfect Intro — Will Have + Past Participle The future perfect talks about something that will be finished before a time in the future.

Form: will have + past participle. It is almost always used with by + a future time: “By next year, I will have saved enough money for an emergency.” (The saving will be finished before next year.) — “By June, she will have paid all her debts.” — “By 2028, they will have helped their children through school.” Compare the three times: past habit (I used to worry), present change (now I save every month), future result (by next year, I will have saved enough). Together they tell the whole story of a changed life.
grammar.lesson: Bài 10: Tiền Bạc, Công Việc & Sự Thỏa Lòng

grammar.title: Wish + past (present wishes: I wish I could speak better English; I wish the church had more workers); third conditional intro (If + past perfect, would have + past participle: If Jonah had obeyed God at first, he would have gone to Nineveh at once)
grammar.explain:
Structure 1: Wish + Past — Present Wishes Use wish + past simple to talk about something you want to be different now: “I wish I could speak better English.” — “I wish our church had more workers for the harvest.” — “I wish I knew more about the nations.” Notice: although we use the past form, the meaning is present. Could is very common here: wish + could + verb means “I want to be able to…”.

Use wish + would + verb for a wish about the future, or a wish that someone else would change: “I wish God would send more workers into His harvest.” — “I wish my neighbours would listen to the good news.”

Use wish + past perfect (had + past participle) for a wish about the past — something that already happened and cannot change: “I wish Jonah had obeyed God at first.” — “I wish I had studied English earlier.”

Structure 2: Third Conditional — If + Past Perfect, Would Have + Past Participle The third conditional talks about an unreal past — something that did NOT happen, and its imaginary result.

Form: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle. Examples: “If Jonah had obeyed God at first, he would have gone to Nineveh at once.” (But he did not obey at first — he fled to Tarshish.) — “If the people of Nineveh had not repented, God would have destroyed the city.” (But they did repent, so God showed mercy.)

The two halves can change places: “Jonah would not have spent three days in the fish if he had obeyed God at first.” Use the negative forms to show the opposite of what really happened: had not fled / would not have been thrown into the sea.

Watch out: never use would in the if clause — say “If Jonah had obeyed…”, not “If Jonah would have obeyed…”. And remember: wish + past is about the present (“I wish I could speak better now”), while the third conditional is about the past (“If I had studied earlier, I would have spoken better then”).
grammar.lesson: Bài 11: Sứ Mạng Đến Với Muôn Dân

grammar.title: Capstone review: present simple/continuous, past simple/continuous/perfect, present perfect, future will/going to, future perfect (intro), conditionals 1-3 recap, passive recap.
grammar.explain:
This lesson adds no new grammar point. Instead, we review everything from Lessons 01–11 in one table. The question to ask about every sentence is: when does it happen, and is it finished? If you can answer those two questions, you can choose the right form.

Mixing tenses in one story: “John saw (past simple) a new heaven. The first heaven had passed (past perfect) away. Jesus has risen (present perfect), so we have (present simple) a living hope today. One day, God will wipe (future) away every tear.”

Practise telling Revelation 21 in four tenses: what John saw (past), what is true now (present perfect), what God will do (future), and what will already be finished by then (future perfect).

Watch out: (1) never use will after if in a Type 1 conditional — say “If we trust God, He will guard us.” (2) Present perfect needs has/have — “Jesus has risen.” (3) Future perfect needs a future time marker — “By the time Jesus returns, …” or “By then, …”.
grammar.lesson: Bài 12: Khải Huyền và Hy Vọng Sống Động — Ôn Tập Tổng Kết

grammar.title: Perfect continuous tenses: present perfect continuous (have/has been + verb-ing) and past perfect continuous (had been + verb-ing)
grammar.explain:
Form. Present perfect continuous: have / has + been + verb-ing. Past perfect continuous: had + been + verb-ing. Example: I have been living here for five years. They had been waiting for the Messiah for many years before Jesus came.

Use 1 — an action that started in the past and is still going on. Present perfect continuous stresses the activity and its duration, not the finished result. Use it with for (a length of time) and since (a starting point). Example: She has been studying English since 2020. We have been praying for our city all year.

Use 2 — a recent activity with a visible result now. Example: I have been reading First Peter this week, so my Bible is full of notes. Your eyes are red — have you been crying? The continuous form explains the present situation.

Present perfect continuous or present perfect simple? Use the continuous when you want to stress how long the activity has lasted. Use the simple when you want to stress the completed result or the number of times. Compare: I have been writing letters all morning (the activity lasted all morning) with I have written three letters this morning (the finished result: three letters).

Use 3 — past perfect continuous: a longer action that was in progress before another past event. The longer action uses had been + verb-ing; the shorter, later event uses the past simple. Example: The fishermen had been working all night before Jesus came to them. The believers had been praying together when the Spirit came.

Watch out — stative verbs. Verbs that describe a state, not an action, are not used in continuous forms: know, believe, belong, love, hate, understand, need, want. Say I have known him for years, not I have been knowing him for years. Say We have belonged to this church since 2019, not We have been belonging.

Common mistake. Do not use the present continuous for a long duration that reaches the present. Wrong: I am living here for five years. Right: I have been living here for five years. The present continuous (I am living here now) describes only this moment; the perfect continuous connects the past to the present.
examples: I have been living in Hanoi for five years.
She has been studying English since 2020.
They have been waiting for the bus for an hour.
We have been praying for our city all year.
I have been reading First Peter this week.
The fishermen had been working all night before Jesus came to them.
The believers had been praying together when the Spirit came.
He had been walking to the temple every day before he met Philip.
grammar.lesson: Bài 1: Sống Như Khách Lạ Trên Đất

grammar.title: Conditionals type 3 and mixed conditionals: past regrets, past causes with present results, present causes with past results
grammar.explain:
Type 3 — a past that cannot be changed. Form: If + past perfect, would have + past participle. Example: If Paul had given up, we would never have read these words. Both parts refer to the past, and both are impossible now: Paul did not give up, and we did read the words. Type 3 is the grammar of regret and of thankfulness for what did happen.

Mixed conditional 1 — a past cause with a present result. Form: If + past perfect, would + base verb. Example: If my mother had not taught me to pray, I would not know where to turn now. The cause is in the past (she taught me), but the result is now (I know where to turn). Use this form when a past event still shapes the present.

Mixed conditional 2 — a present cause with a past result. Form: If + past simple, would have + past participle. Example: If I were stronger now, I would have helped you yesterday. The cause is present (I am not strong now), but the result is past (I did not help yesterday). This form is less common, but it is exactly what you need when you explain a past failure by a present fact.

Watch out — never use would in the if-clause. Wrong: If I would have known, I would have come. Right: If I had known, I would have come. Would belongs only in the result clause. For possibility instead of certainty, use could have or might have: If he had asked, God might have given him wisdom.

Using conditionals to talk about the Bible. Type 3 retells past events: If Joseph had not trusted God, he would have given up in prison. Mixed conditionals apply the past to the present: If God had not loved us, we would have no hope today. If Christ had not risen, our faith would be in vain.
examples: If Paul had given up, we would never have read these words.
If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
If my mother had not taught me to pray, I would not know where to turn now.
If I were stronger now, I would have helped you yesterday.
If he had saved money last year, he would be rich now.
If they had listened to the warning, they would not be in trouble now.
If God had not loved us, we would have no hope at all.
If Joseph had not trusted God, he would have given up in prison.
grammar.lesson: Bài 2: Đau Khổ và Hy Vọng

grammar.title: Modals of deduction and speculation: must / can't / may / might / could (present) and must have / can't have / might have + past participle (past)
grammar.explain:
Present deduction — how sure are you? Must + base verb means I am sure it is true: He must be a wise man. Can't + base verb means I am sure it is NOT true: She can't have decided yet. May, might, and could + base verb mean it is possible, but I am not sure: It might be God's will, or it might not.

Past deduction — looking back. Must have + past participle means I am sure it happened: They must have wanted you very much. Can't have + past participle means I am sure it did NOT happen: She can't have decided at once. Might have or may have + past participle means it is possible it happened: The news might have been good.

Must for deduction is not must for obligation. Compare: You must pray (obligation — you have to pray) with He must be wise (deduction — I am sure he is wise). The same word has two jobs, and the context tells you which one it is. Do not confuse them.

Choosing the strength. Must and can't claim 90 to 100 percent certainty. May, might, and could claim only possibility. Saying It must be God's will claims that you are certain about God's will — be careful with that claim. Saying It might be God's will is humbler, and usually wiser.

Asking about the past. To question a past deduction, use Can he have...? or Could he have...? Example: Can he have forgotten the meeting? To soften a deduction, add Do you think...? Example: Do you think it might be God's will? Softening is a mark of wisdom in English: it leaves room for other people to disagree.
examples: He listens before he speaks. He must be a wise man.
She is still praying. She can't have decided yet.
It might be God's will, or it might not.
They must have wanted you very much.
He must have been a patient man.
The roads are wet. It must have rained last night.
She is smiling. The news might have been good.
He can't have read Proverbs 3, or he would trust God more.
grammar.lesson: Bài 3: Sự Khôn Ngoan Cho Quyết Định

grammar.title: Advanced passive: reporting verbs (It is said that... / He is said to...) and causative have / get (have something done; get someone to do something)
grammar.explain:
Reporting passive 1 — It is said / thought / believed that + clause. Use it when you report what people say in general, without naming anyone: It is said that what we watch shapes what we think. It is more formal and more careful than People say... — and it is the form you will meet in news reports, academic writing, and sermons.

Reporting passive 2 — subject + is said / thought / believed to + base verb (present) or to have + past participle (past). He is said to be a wise teacher. Paul is believed to have written Philippians from prison. The second form (to have + past participle) reports a past event: She is thought to have written the letter in Rome.

Causative have / get + object + past participle. You arrange for someone else to do something for you: I had my phone repaired last week. I paid someone to repair it; I did not repair it myself. Get is more informal and more common in speech: She got her hair cut yesterday.

Causative have / get + person + verb. Two patterns, and they are different: have + person + base verb (I had the teacher explain the verse — no to), and get + person + to + verb (I got the teacher to explain the verse). Do not mix them: had him to explain is wrong, and got him explain is wrong.

Why use the passive here? The passive lets you talk about ideas without blaming or naming people. It is thought that our habits shape our minds is gentler than People think... — useful when you discuss sensitive topics in the church, and it is the mark of a careful, B2-level writer.
examples: It is said that what we watch shapes what we think.
It is thought that our habits shape our minds more than our wishes do.
He is said to be a wise teacher.
She is thought to know the Bible well.
Paul is believed to have written Philippians from prison.
I had my phone repaired last week.
She got her hair cut yesterday.
I got the teacher to explain the verse again.
grammar.lesson: Bài 4: Tâm Trí Của Cơ Đốc Nhân

grammar.title: Noun clauses (that / what / whether / if) and cleft sentences for emphasis (It is... who/that... / What... is...)
grammar.explain:
Noun clauses — a clause that works like a noun. That-clauses follow verbs of saying and believing: Jesus said that the greatest must be the servant. Paul teaches that an overseer must be above reproach. In speech, that can be dropped: Jesus said the greatest must be the servant.

Wh-clauses — what, who, why, how + clause. What matters most is character. I don't know why he wants to be a leader. Note the word order: a noun clause uses statement order, not question order. Say I don't know why he wants to be a leader, not I don't know why does he want to be a leader.

Whether and if clauses. I don't know whether he will be a good leader. Whether is more formal than if. Use whether after prepositions and before infinitives: the question of whether to choose him, I don't know whether to stay or go.

It-clefts for emphasis. Form: It + be + stressed part + who / that + rest of the sentence. It was Jesus who turned leadership upside down. The cleft puts a spotlight on one part of the sentence: not Paul, not Peter — Jesus. Use it when you want to correct someone or to underline the point of a sermon.

What-clefts for emphasis. Form: What + clause + be + stressed part. What matters most is character. What Paul requires is an overseer above reproach. Use clefts sparingly: one cleft in a paragraph gives it power; five clefts in a paragraph make it sound strange.
examples: Jesus said that the greatest must be the servant.
What matters most is character, not talent.
It was Jesus who turned leadership upside down.
It is the servant who is truly great.
What Paul requires is an overseer above reproach.
I don't know whether he will be a good leader.
I wonder who the church will choose.
It is gentleness that shows a leader's heart.
grammar.lesson: Bài 5: Lãnh Đạo và Phục Vụ

grammar.title: Discourse markers for argumentation (however, furthermore, on the other hand, in contrast, nevertheless) and concession clauses (although / even though / despite / in spite of)
grammar.explain:
Discourse markers — words that show how your ideas connect. However means but, in a formal way: Some laughed. However, some believed. Furthermore means and also, more strongly: Paul listened first. Furthermore, he proclaimed the truth. On the other hand gives the opposite view. In contrast gives the direct opposite. Nevertheless means despite that.

Position and punctuation. Markers usually come at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma: However, some believed. In the middle of a sentence, use two commas: Some, however, believed. Never write however without a comma after it at the start of a sentence.

Concession with although and even though. Although / even though + clause (with a verb): Although many people worshipped many gods, Paul showed them the one true God. Even though is stronger than although: it concedes something surprising. Even though some people laughed, Paul kept preaching.

Concession with despite and in spite of. Despite / in spite of + noun or verb-ing: Despite being alone, Paul spoke boldly. Do not mix the two patterns: Despite Paul was alone is wrong, and Although being alone is wrong. Although needs a verb; despite needs a noun or an -ing form.

Arguing gently. Use concession to agree before you disagree: Although I understand your view, I believe Christ is the only way. This is how Paul argued in Athens, and it is how Peter tells us to answer: with gentleness and respect.
examples: Some laughed. However, some believed.
Paul listened first. Furthermore, he proclaimed the truth.
Although many people worshipped many gods, Paul showed them the one true God.
Despite being alone in Athens, Paul spoke boldly.
Even though some people laughed, Paul kept preaching.
My colleague is kind. On the other hand, she does not believe in Christ.
In contrast to the many gods of Athens, the true God made the world.
Although I understand your view, I believe Christ is the only way.
grammar.lesson: Bài 6: Truyền Giáo Trong Thế Giới Đa Nguyên

passages.title: Bài 1: Bài Giảng Trên Núi
sentences: One day, large crowds followed Jesus up a mountainside.
He sat down, His disciples came to Him, and He began to teach them.
These words, in Matthew 5 to 7, are called the Sermon on the Mount, and they are the most famous teaching in the world.
Jesus began with the Beatitudes, eight promises of blessing.
He said that God blesses the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, and those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.
The world says that the rich, the strong, and the famous are blessed.
Jesus says the opposite: God blesses the humble people who know they need Him.
Then Jesus gave His followers two pictures of their life in the world.
They are the salt of the earth: just as salt gives flavor to food and keeps it from rotting, Christians should make life better for everyone around them.
They are also the light of the world: just as a lamp on a hill cannot be hidden, a Christian life cannot be hidden.
Their good works should shine before others so that people give glory to God.
Jesus also taught His disciples how to pray.
He gave them the Lord's Prayer, which begins with God's name and God's kingdom, and only then asks for daily bread, forgiveness, and protection from temptation.
He warned them not to pray like hypocrites who love to be seen by others.
Finally, Jesus taught about treasures.
Earthly treasures are destroyed by moth and rust and stolen by thieves, but treasures in heaven last forever.
'For where your treasure is,' Jesus said, 'there your heart will be also.

questions.q: 1. According to Matthew 5:3-10, who receives the kingdom of heaven?
questions.a: The poor in spirit.

questions.q: 2. Why does Jesus call His followers 'the salt of the earth' and 'the light of the world'?
questions.a: Because, like salt and light, Christians should make a real difference in the world: salt preserves and gives flavor, light shows the way and cannot be hidden.

questions.q: 3. What does Jesus teach about prayer in Matthew 6:9-13?
questions.a: He teaches His disciples to pray to 'Our Father in heaven', to honor God's name, to ask for His kingdom and will, for daily bread, for forgiveness, and for deliverance from temptation and evil.

questions.q: 4. According to Matthew 6:19-21, where should we store our treasures, and why?
questions.a: In heaven, because earthly treasures are destroyed by moth and rust and stolen by thieves, but heavenly treasures last forever; and where our treasure is, there our heart will be also.

passages.title: Bài 2: Cuộc Đời Đa-vít
sentences: David was the youngest of Jesse’s eight sons, and nobody expected him to become king.
While his older brothers joined King Saul’s army, David stayed home and looked after his father’s sheep.
It taught him two things: how to fight wild animals, and how to trust God.
When a lion or a bear attacked the flock, David fought it and saved the sheep.
One day, the prophet Samuel came to Bethlehem.
God had told Samuel to anoint a new king, and Samuel had already looked at David’s seven older brothers.
But God said, “Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.
” So Samuel sent for David and anointed him king of Israel.
God had chosen the youngest son, the one with a humble and faithful heart.
Later, Israel faced the Philistines, whose champion was a giant named Goliath.
For forty days, Goliath had shouted his challenge, and no soldier in Israel had dared to fight him.
Then David arrived, and he heard the giant’s voice.
“I will fight him,” David said.
He refused Saul’s heavy armour — it was too big for him — and took his sling and five smooth stones from the stream, ran toward Goliath, and struck him down with one stone.
The battle belonged to the LORD.
But David was not perfect.
Years later, he sinned against God and Uriah, and tried to hide his sin.
God sent Nathan, and David repented.
He prayed the words of Psalm 51: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.
” David was called “a man after God’s own heart” — not because he never sinned, but because he always came back to God in repentance and trusted in His mercy.

questions.q: 1. What two things did David’s job as a shepherd teach him?
questions.a: How to fight wild animals, and how to trust God.

questions.q: 2. Why did God choose David instead of his older brothers?
questions.a: God looks on the heart, not on outward appearance; David had a humble and faithful heart.

questions.q: 3. Why did David refuse to wear Saul’s armour?
questions.a: Saul’s armour was too big for him, so he refused to wear it.

questions.q: 4. What does the passage say was the reason David was called “a man after God’s own heart”?
questions.a: Not because he never sinned, but because he always came back to God in repentance and trusted in His mercy.

passages.title: Bài 3: Các Tiên Tri: Ê-sai
sentences: Isaiah lived about seven hundred years before Jesus was born.
God called him to be a prophet, a man who speaks God's words to God's people.
Isaiah warned Israel about its sins, but he also gave the people wonderful promises about the future.
His greatest prophecy is about the Servant of the Lord, in chapter 53.
The Servant was not a king in a palace.
He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief.
He was wounded for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities.
The punishment that brought us peace was laid on Him, and by His wounds we are healed.
Isaiah's words were written long before Jesus came, but Christians believe they describe Jesus on the cross.
Jesus took our place.
He was pierced for our sins, and because He suffered, we can be forgiven and have peace with God.
Then, in chapter 55, God gives a free invitation: "Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters.
" Forgiveness cannot be bought.
It is given by grace to everyone who comes.
Isaiah says we should seek the Lord while He may be found, and forsake our wicked ways and return to Him.
God will have mercy on us, and He will abundantly pardon.
The Servant suffered, so that we could be invited home.
When we read Isaiah today, we are reading a letter written to people long ago, yet it speaks directly to us: our sins were carried by Another, and God's door stands open to everyone who will come.

vocab.vi: Sự vi phạm, sự phạm tội
Bị nghiền nát, bị đè bẹp
Bị khinh bỉ, bị khinh thường
Bị chối bỏ, bị từ bỏ

questions.q: 1. When did Isaiah live, and who was he?
questions.a: About 700 years before Jesus; a prophet who spoke God's word to Israel.

questions.q: 2. What did the Servant suffer, according to Isaiah 53:5?
questions.a: He was wounded for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities.

questions.q: 3. What does 'by His wounds we are healed' mean?
questions.a: Because Jesus suffered in our place, we can be forgiven and have peace with God.

questions.q: 4. How is God's invitation in Isaiah 55 different from buying something in a shop?
questions.a: It is completely free — no money, no cost; forgiveness is given by grace.

passages.title: Bài 4: Sự Khôn Ngoan: Châm Ngôn & Thi Thiên
sentences: Solomon became king of Israel when he was still young.
One night God said to him, "Ask what I shall give you.
" Solomon did not ask for riches or a long life.
He asked for wisdom — a heart that could judge God's people rightly.
God was pleased, and gave Solomon great wisdom — and riches and honour as well.
Proverbs collects the wisdom that Solomon and other wise men taught in Israel.
Its first words tell us its purpose: to know wisdom, to understand words of insight.
The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
A wise person listens to counsel; a foolish person trusts only his own opinion.
The Psalms sing the same wisdom: Psalm 1 pictures the wise person as a tree planted by streams of water.
He does not walk in the counsel of the wicked; his delight is in the law of the Lord, and he meditates on it day and night.
His leaf does not wither.
Psalm 19 says the law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul; it makes wise the simple, rejoices the heart, and enlightens the eyes.
God's words are more to be desired than gold, sweeter than honey.
And Psalm 119 gives the most famous picture of all: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.
" God's word does not show us the whole road, but it shows us the next step — enough light to walk by.
Proverbs adds: the name of the Lord is a strong tower, and the righteous run into it and are safe; and iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another.
Wisdom grows when we trust the Lord, listen to His word, and walk with friends who tell the truth.

vocab.vi: Nơi nương náu, nơi ẩn náu
Sự dạy dỗ, lời chỉ dạy
Sự hiểu biết, sự thông sáng
Niềm vui thích, sự vui mừng

questions.q: 1. What did Solomon ask God for, and why?
questions.a: Solomon asked God for wisdom to lead Israel, not for riches or a long life, and God gave him wisdom and much more.

questions.q: 2. In Psalm 1, what is the wise person like?
questions.a: Like a tree planted by streams of water — its leaf does not wither.

questions.q: 3. What does Psalm 19 say God's perfect law does?
questions.a: It makes wise the simple, it rejoices the heart, and it enlightens the eyes.

questions.q: 4. What does the picture of a lamp in Psalm 119:105 teach us about God's word?
questions.a: God's word shows us the way to walk — a lamp for our feet and a light for our path — when the way is dark.

questions.q: 5. What two pictures in Proverbs show us where wisdom and safety are found?
questions.a: The righteous are safe because they run to the Lord's name, a strong tower; wise friends sharpen each other like iron sharpens iron.

passages.title: Bài 5: Rô-ma: Được Xưng Công Chính Bởi Đức Tin
sentences: Romans is Paul's greatest letter, and its heart is a question: how can a sinful person be right with a holy God?
Paul's answer is clear: no one can earn God's favour by keeping the law.
All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
The law shows us our sin, but it cannot save us.
If we were justified by works, grace would not be grace, and boasting would be possible.
But God has made another way.
The righteousness of God has been revealed apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe.
God put forward Jesus as a propitiation by His blood, to be received by faith.
On the cross, Jesus took the punishment our sins deserved, so that God can be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.
Paul proves this from Abraham.
Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
Abraham lived about four hundred years before the law was given, so he could not have been saved by keeping the law.
He was saved by faith, and so are we.
God counts faith as righteousness for everyone who trusts in Christ.
Then Paul tells us what justification changes.
Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
We have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God.
Hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts.
And the greatest proof of that love is this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
If we trusted in our own works, we would never know if we had done enough.
But because we trust in Jesus, we can rest in peace.

vocab.vi: Được kể là, được tính là
Sự đến gần, quyền tiếp cận

questions.q: 1. According to the passage, why can no one earn God's favour by keeping the law?
questions.a: No one can be justified by works, because all have sinned and no one keeps the law perfectly.

questions.q: 2. How was Abraham justified, and why does the timing matter?
questions.a: He believed God's promise, and God counted his faith as righteousness — about 400 years before the law was given.

questions.q: 3. What does it mean to be justified?
questions.a: To be declared righteous by God, as if we had never sinned; it is a free gift of grace through faith in Christ.

questions.q: 4. What four blessings does Romans 5 say belong to those who are justified by faith?
questions.a: Peace with God, access into grace, hope of God's glory, and hope that does not put us to shame — even in suffering.

passages.title: Bài 6: Các Dụ Ngôn Về Nước Thiên Đàng
sentences: Jesus loved to teach with parables — short, simple stories that carry a deep truth about the kingdom of heaven.
He told His disciples that the kingdom is like a sower who went out to sow his seed.
Some seed fell along the path, and the birds ate it.
Some fell on rocky ground, where it grew quickly but had no root, so the sun burned it.
Some fell among thorns, and the thorns choked it.
But some seed fell on good soil, and it gave a rich harvest — a hundred, sixty, or thirty times as much as was sown.
The seed is the word of God, and the soil is the heart that hears it.
Then Jesus said that the kingdom is like a grain of mustard seed.
It is the smallest of all seeds, yet when it grows, it becomes the largest of all garden plants, and the birds come and rest in its branches.
The kingdom starts small, but it grows very great.
He also said that the kingdom is like treasure hidden in a field.
When a man found it, he sold all that he had and bought that field.
It is also like a merchant who found one pearl of great value, and sold everything to buy it.
The kingdom is worth everything we have.
In Matthew 25, Jesus told two more parables about being ready.
Ten virgins waited for the bridegroom, but only five were wise and took oil for their lamps.
And a master gave his servants talents and asked them to use his money well.
The faithful servants were rewarded, and the master said, 'Well done, good and faithful servant.
' The parables ask us a question: what kind of soil are we, and are we ready for the King?

questions.q: 1. Why did Jesus teach in parables?
questions.a: He teaches with short stories (parables) that show what the kingdom of heaven is like, so that ordinary people can understand deep truths.

questions.q: 2. What does the mustard seed teach us about the kingdom of heaven?
questions.a: It grows from the smallest seed into the largest garden plant — the kingdom starts small but grows very great.

questions.q: 3. What did the man who found the treasure and the merchant who found the pearl have in common?
questions.a: Both the man and the merchant sold everything they had, because the kingdom is worth more than anything else.

questions.q: 4. What is the difference between the wise and the foolish virgins?
questions.a: Five were wise and took oil for their lamps; five were foolish and took no oil, so they were not ready when the bridegroom came.

questions.q: 5. What did the master do when he returned in the parable of the talents?
questions.a: He rewarded the faithful servants, who had used his gifts well, and said, 'Well done, good and faithful servant.'

passages.title: Bài 7: Đức Thánh Linh Trong Sách Công Vụ Các Sứ Đồ
sentences: Fifty days after Jesus rose from the dead, the day of Pentecost arrived.
The believers were all together in one place in Jerusalem, waiting and praying as Jesus had told them to do.
Suddenly, a sound like a mighty rushing wind came from heaven and filled the whole house where they were sitting.
Tongues of fire appeared and rested on each one of them.
The Holy Spirit came upon them, and they were all filled with power.
They began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit gave them words to speak.
People from many nations were amazed, because each one heard the believers speaking in his own language.
Some people were confused, but Peter stood up with the eleven apostles and spoke out boldly.
He proclaimed that Jesus, whom the people had crucified, is both Lord and Christ.
His words brought conviction to the crowd.
They asked, "What shall we do?
" Peter said, "Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
" About three thousand people were baptized that day, and the church in Jerusalem was born.
Soon after this, Peter and John were arrested and threatened, and the leaders told them not to speak about Jesus anymore.
But the believers did not hide.
They gathered together and prayed: "Lord, give your servants boldness to speak your word.
" As they prayed, the place where they were gathered was shaken.
They were filled with the Holy Spirit again, and they continued to speak the word of God with boldness.
The same Spirit who came at Pentecost still fills God's people today, and He still gives them power to be His witnesses.

questions.q: 1. What happened when the Holy Spirit came on the day of Pentecost?
questions.a: The Holy Spirit came upon the believers, and they were filled with power and began to speak in other languages.

questions.q: 2. What did Peter do when he stood up before the crowd?
questions.a: He stood up and proclaimed that Jesus is Lord and Christ, and he called the crowd to repent and be baptized.

questions.q: 3. What was the result of Peter's sermon?
questions.a: About three thousand people received his word and were baptized that day.

questions.q: 4. What did the believers do in Acts 4 after Peter and John were threatened?
questions.a: They prayed together, asking God for boldness to speak His word, and the place where they were gathered was shaken.

questions.q: 5. What happened after the believers prayed?
questions.a: They were filled with the Holy Spirit again and continued to speak the word of God with boldness.

passages.title: Bài 8: Cầu Nguyện Và Thờ Phượng
sentences: Psalm 95 begins with a joyful invitation: “Oh come, let us sing to the LORD; let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation!
” Then it gives the reason: the Lord is a great God and a great King above all gods.
He made the sea and the dry land, and we are the people of His pasture, the sheep of His hand.
So the psalm says, “Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker!
” True worship begins with knowing who God is — and who we are.
We should come to Him with a humble heart, because He is holy and we are small.
We ought to thank Him for His goodness before we ask Him for anything.
And we must remember that worship is not only singing; it is a whole life offered to God.
In John 4, Jesus met a Samaritan woman at a well.
She asked Him where people ought to worship — on the mountain or in Jerusalem.
Jesus answered that true worshipers must worship the Father in spirit and truth.
To worship in spirit means to worship with a sincere heart, not just with words or a ceremony.
To worship in truth means to worship God as He really is, not as we imagine Him.
The Father is seeking such people to worship Him.
God might answer our prayers in a way we do not expect, but He always hears us.
So we should pray every day, we ought to confess our sins honestly, and we must never worship with a proud heart.
When we come to God in spirit and truth, we find what the woman at the well found: living water, and a Saviour who knows us completely and loves us still.

vocab.vi: Tôn thờ, yêu mến hết lòng

questions.q: 1. According to Psalm 95, why should we worship the Lord?
questions.a: Because the Lord is a great God and a great King, and He made us — He is our Maker.

questions.q: 2. According to John 4:20, what did the Samaritan woman ask Jesus?
questions.a: Where people ought to worship — on the mountain or in Jerusalem.

questions.q: 3. According to John 4:24, how must those who worship God worship Him?
questions.a: They must worship the Father in spirit and truth.

questions.q: 4. According to John 4:23, whom is the Father seeking?
questions.a: The Father is seeking such people to worship Him.

questions.q: 5. According to John 4:25–26, what did the woman say, and how did Jesus answer?
questions.a: The woman said, “I know that Messiah is coming,” and Jesus answered, “I who speak to you am He.”

passages.title: Bài 9: Hội Thánh: Một Thân Thể
sentences: The church is not a building.
The church is a body — the body of Christ.
In 1 Corinthians 12, Paul says that just as a human body has many members, so it is with Christ.
The eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of you.
" The head cannot say to the feet, "I have no need of you.
" Every member is needed, and every member is important.
God has given different gifts to different people.
Some are apostles, some are prophets, some are teachers.
Some have the gift of serving, and some have the gift of encouraging others.
No gift is small, and no member is unimportant.
If one member suffers, all suffer together.
If one member is honoured, all rejoice together.
In Ephesians 4, Paul writes that Christ gave these gifts to His people to build up the body, until we all reach unity in the faith and grow up into maturity.
We must learn to speak the truth in love, so that the whole body grows.
When each member does its part, the body builds itself up in love.
There is one body and one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all.
That is the unity we must keep.
We enjoy serving together, and we want to grow together.
God called us to love one another, to encourage one another, and to build one another up.
That is what it means to be the church — one body, many members, working together in love.

vocab.vi: Quyền làm đầu, sự lãnh đạo

questions.q: 1. Why does Paul compare the church to a body?
questions.a: Because, like a body, the church has many different members, and every member is needed and important.

questions.q: 2. According to 1 Corinthians 12, what happens when one member suffers?
questions.a: All the members suffer together with it.

questions.q: 3. According to Ephesians 4, why did Christ give gifts to His people?
questions.a: To equip the saints and to build up the body of Christ, until we all reach unity in the faith and grow up into maturity.

questions.q: 4. What does it mean to "speak the truth in love" (Ephesians 4:15)?
questions.a: It means we tell each other the truth in a loving way, so that the whole body grows up into Christ.

questions.q: 5. How many bodies, Spirits, Lords, and faiths does Paul name in Ephesians 4:4-6?
questions.a: One of each: one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.

passages.title: Bài 10: Tiền Bạc, Công Việc & Sự Thỏa Lòng
sentences: Lan used to worry about money all the time.
Every night, she would check her bank account on her phone, and she would think about tomorrow.
Would she have enough?
Would she lose her job?
She worked hard, but her money always seemed to run away.
One Sunday, her pastor read the words of Jesus: 'Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal.
But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven.
' Lan listened carefully.
Jesus also said, 'Do not be anxious about your life.
Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them.
Are you not of more value than they?
' Lan thought about her grandmother, who had never been rich.
Every month, her grandmother would save a little money, and she would give some of it to help her neighbours.
'God gives us our daily bread,' she used to say.
'Enough is enough.
' Lan decided to change.
She made a simple budget.
She saved a little every month, and she gave a little to help others.
She stopped checking her bank account every night.
By next year, she will have saved enough money for an emergency, and she plans to help her younger sister with her school fees.
Lan is learning contentment.
She cannot serve both God and money, so she has chosen her Master.
Money is a good servant, but it is a bad master.
'Do not be anxious about tomorrow,' Jesus said, 'for tomorrow will be anxious for itself.
Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.

vocab.vi: Kho báu, của cải quý giá
Sự thỏa lòng, sự bằng lòng
Sự tin kính, lòng đạo đức
Bánh hằng ngày, nhu cầu hằng ngày
Ngân sách, kế hoạch chi tiêu

questions.q: 1. How did Lan worry about money before she learned contentment?
questions.a: She used to check her bank account every night and worry about tomorrow — whether she would have enough, and whether she would lose her job.

questions.q: 2. What did Lan's grandmother do with her money?
questions.a: She saved a little money every month, gave some to help others, and said, 'God gives us our daily bread. Enough is enough.'

questions.q: 3. What does Jesus say about the birds in Matthew 6:26?
questions.a: The birds do not store up food, but God feeds them; Jesus says we are more valuable than the birds, so God will take care of us too.

questions.q: 4. Can we serve both God and money? Why not?
questions.a: No — Jesus says we cannot serve both God and money; money is a good servant, but it is a bad master.

questions.q: 5. What will Lan have saved by next year, and what does she plan to do with her savings?
questions.a: By next year she will have saved enough for an emergency, and she plans to help her younger sister with school fees.

passages.title: Bài 11: Sứ Mạng Đến Với Muôn Dân
sentences: After Jesus rose from the dead, He met His disciples on a mountain in Galilee.
He said, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.
Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you.
And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
' This is the Great Commission.
Jesus also said, 'You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.
' A witness tells others what he has seen and heard.
We are His witnesses, first in our own city, then to the nations.
The Old Testament already shows God's heart for the nations.
God sent the prophet Jonah to Nineveh, a great city of Gentiles, to preach repentance.
But Jonah was reluctant.
He did not want God to show mercy to Nineveh, so he fled to Tarshish, in the opposite direction.
God sent a great fish.
After three days, the fish brought Jonah back to dry land, and he went to Nineveh.
The people repented, and God showed them mercy.
Jonah was angry, but God asked him, 'Should I not pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 people?
' God's heart is for all nations.
God can use even a reluctant witness.
Today the harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few.
We can begin where we are: tell our neighbours about Jesus, pray for the nations, and go wherever God sends us.
Jesus is with us always, to the end of the age.

vocab.vi: Sứ mạng, công tác truyền giáo
Làm phép báp-têm, chịu phép báp-têm
Dân ngoại (người không phải Do Thái)

questions.q: 1. Why can Jesus send His disciples to all nations?
questions.a: Because Jesus said, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me,' and on that authority He sends His disciples to all nations.

questions.q: 2. What are the disciples told to do in Matthew 28:19-20?
questions.a: To make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey everything Jesus commanded.

questions.q: 3. According to Acts 1:8, what will happen when the Holy Spirit comes upon the disciples?
questions.a: The Holy Spirit gives them power, and they will be His witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

questions.q: 4. Why did Jonah flee to Tarshish instead of obeying God?
questions.a: He was reluctant. He did not want God to show mercy to the people of Nineveh, so he fled to Tarshish.

questions.q: 5. What happened when Jonah finally preached in Nineveh?
questions.a: The people repented, and God showed them mercy and did not destroy the city.

passages.title: Bài 12: Khải Huyền và Hy Vọng Sống Động — Ôn Tập Tổng Kết
sentences: A Living Hope for a New World.
Nearly two thousand years ago, the apostle John was living in exile on the small island of Patmos.
But one day, God gave him a wonderful vision.
John saw a new heaven and a new earth, because the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.
He saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven, prepared as a bride.
Then he heard a loud voice from the throne: 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man.
He will dwell with them, and they will be his people.
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more.
' Before John's vision, the apostle Peter had written about the same hope.
Peter said that God has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.
Because Jesus has risen, our hope is alive.
We have an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for us.
By God's power, we are being guarded through faith for a salvation that will be revealed in the last time.
Peter was honest: for a little while we may be grieved by various trials.
Trials test our faith, and our faith is more precious than gold.
But one day, the testing will end.
In the new city, the river of the water of life will flow from the throne of God, and the tree of life will bear fruit every month.
Night will be no more, and the Lord God will be our light.
We will reign with him forever and ever.
That is why we can rejoice today, even in trials.
The story is not over yet, but we know how it ends: God will make all things new.

questions.q: 1. Where was John living when God gave him the vision?
questions.a: On the small island of Patmos, in exile.

questions.q: 2. What did John see coming down from heaven?
questions.a: The holy city, the new Jerusalem, prepared as a bride for her husband.

questions.q: 3. Why is our hope called a 'living hope'?
questions.a: Because Jesus has risen from the dead; our hope is alive because He is alive.

questions.q: 4. What three words does Peter use to describe our inheritance?
questions.a: Imperishable, undefiled, and unfading.

questions.q: 5. What will there be no more of in the new city?
questions.a: Death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more; night will be no more, and the Lord God will be our light.

passages.title: Bài 1: Sống Như Khách Lạ Trên Đất
sentences: Peter wrote his first letter to Christians who were scattered across Asia Minor, far from Jerusalem and far from home.
They were strangers in the cities where they lived.
They had no power, no protection, and no permanent place.
Some of them were suffering because of their faith.
Peter did not tell them to fight for a home on earth.
Instead, he told them about a better home.
God, in his great mercy, had caused them to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.
Their inheritance was imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for them.
No thief could steal it, no fire could burn it, and no time could make it fade.
While they waited, God himself was guarding them by his power through faith.
Their trials were real, and Peter did not pretend otherwise.
He said their faith was being tested like gold in fire, and tested faith is more precious than gold.
Peter also told them who they were: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession.
God had called them out of darkness into his marvelous light so that they would proclaim his excellencies.
And because they belonged to God, they were to live differently.
